title: Why a Leader's Blind Spot Often Grows
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that leaders' blind spots grow less because their effects compound than because the leaders unknowingly feed them. Leaders lean into whatever they believe made them successful, and drawing on Kaplan and Kaiser's executive assessments the piece notes that the usual problem is a strength overused in nearly every situation. Seniority makes this worse, as leaders receive less candid feedback and read the silence as confirmation, while research on power suggests that recalling a time of power reduces how much people consider others' views. Leaders also build teams in their own image, so the evidence around them keeps confirming the blind spot, as in the example of a decisive leader whose team learns that raising concerns slows things down. The remedy is not more self-reflection but asking people outside the inner circle, such as peers, coaches and HR, a specific question: what do I do too much of? The piece ends by saying leaders cannot eliminate blind spots, only keep them small enough to see.
points: The piece's counterintuitive claim is that blind spots grow because leaders feed them by doubling down on perceived strengths, not because the effects compound by themselves.
Seniority and power reduce candid feedback and the habit of considering others' views, so silence from the team is easily misread as agreement.
The decisive leader example shows the loop: a team of fast deciders learns that concerns slow things down, concerns stop, and the leader moves faster still.
Self-reflection is not the remedy because blind spots are seen by others, so leaders should ask quasi-outsiders such as peers, coaches and HR what they do too much of.
Hiring people who succeed differently and watching where a strength is used everywhere keeps the blind spot small.
quotes: No matter how self-aware a leader is, they are likely to be unaware of a perception others have of them or of an unintended consequence they create. Because blind spots are, by definition, difficult to see, they often remain hidden for months or years without being addressed.
The problem usually isn’t a weakness. It is a strength used too often and in nearly every situation. Such a strength soon costs more than it delivers.
The more senior and experienced a leader becomes, the less candid feedback they receive. They interpret the lack of criticism as confirmation that what they are doing is working.
The leader reads the quiet as alignment and moves faster still. They continue to feed the blind spot because they see it as a strength and everyone around them confirms it.
The remedy is not more reflection. People who spend more time self-reflecting are not necessarily more self-aware. Blind spots are seen by others, so leaders need others to name them.
Peers, executive coaches, and human resources professionals often serve this function. Good leaders ask a very specific question of these quasi-outsiders: “What do I do too much of?
Leaders who stop feeding their blind spots don’t eliminate them. They just keep them small enough to see.
